subject: Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities

messages.author: 4d17bc398c8d91b8
messages.subject: Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
parts:
Hi,

Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year! 

Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:

1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time. 
Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)? 

2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ? 
Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?

Best regards,
Gustaf

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
parts: Hi Gustaf,
On Thu, Apr 16, 2015 at 5:17 PM Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi,

Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year!
That's great. Make sure you're looking at the number of effective sample sizes.

Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:

1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time. 
Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)?

It's a limitation of the current solver we're using, Boost. Nothing in Stan is set is stone, but I don't see us relaxing this anytime soon. What in the model would require times to be identical?

I see wanting to start the initial time at the same time as the first data point (see issue 1340 https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1340), but I haven't seen enough models that providing multiple time points is the right thing to do. If you have a concrete example, that would be interesting to see.

2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ? 
Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?

Yes, time being forced as data will be permanent. One of the other devs (i.e. Michael) might chime in and say otherwise, but I think the problem gets a lot harder when you allow time to be a parameter. (And it's plenty hard now.)

Fortunately, the initial state can be a parameter and the ode function can be written as a function with a lag, so all is not lost. We just won't allow the time itself to be declared as a parameter.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
parts:
Hi!

If your data set has time-points which are the same, then a simple (but tedious) solution would be to stop the integrator each time you have a doublicated time-point in your data and then restart with the last state you got at the next suitable time-point. This could be done in principle by Stan for for the user and this would be really great to have, i.e. a Stan function which stops and starts the ODE solver

- at equal time points
- whenever an event (dosing) occurs

i.e. this would be a convenience function which wraps around the current ODE solver. Since ODEs have the nice property that you can stop and restart at any time, this easy in principle but hard to get it right (carry forward initial state, etc.).

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 4d17bc398c8d91b8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
parts:
Hi Daniel, Bob and Sebastian,

Thanks  for your answers! 

I'm playing around with fitting antibody and nucleic acid kinetic curves to experimental infection data using Lotka-Volterra equations (and I'll make a separate post on my troubles there). In these kinds of studies, observations are often done at regular intervals, e.g. day 1,2,5,10 and 20 post infection for a number of individuals; thus the wish to have multiple observations at the same time point. But it sounds like either jiggling, or just averaging the observations for each timepoint beforehand, would be decent workaround.

If such data are collected in an observational study, there might be an unknown incubation time before symptoms start showing, and so we would have some uncertainty in how long along the kinetic curve we were - but the suggestion of having a "lag" parameter in the diffeq function sounds promising, and I'll give that a go if and when I get far enough to start modelling incubation times.

Best,
Gustaf

parts:
another solution is to run the ODE integrator through the unique set of time-values and later on with some index-fiddling associate the predicted mean value at the time point when you have multiple observations to the same ODE result.

Sebastian

... or you go really hacky and add epsilons to the time-axis to make the observations appear on unique time points. If epsilon is less than 1e-3 of the typical time scale of your problem nothing will change...but then you commit the crime of messing with your input (holy) data.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
parts:
Are you aggregating the individuals somehow?

I'd think that even if you had multiple measurements, you'd
be assuming the diff eq solution would be the same.
That is, y would have K measurements for each time t in (1:T).

data {
vector[K] y[T];
...
}

Then the model has a single solution y_hat giving you expected
individual behavior, then you add noisy measurements (and unexplained
inter-individual variance):

model {

y_hat ~ integrate_ode(...);

for (t in 1:T)
y[t] ~ normal(y_hat[t], sigma_y);
...
}

- Bob
